claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy engineered with stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates is a candidate material for high ductility.
Engineering coherent nanoprecipitates will significantly improve ductility relative to a conventional tungsten-based refractory HEA.
The baseline tungsten-based refractory HEA has high strength but limited ductility.
The baseline alloy's limited ductility is caused by the absence of engineered coherent nanoprecipitates.
Systematic compositional modification can induce stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in a tungsten refractory HEA.
The coherent nanoprecipitates can be produced during standard processing at ambient conditions.
The alloy's tensile ductility should be evaluated at ambient temperature.
Arc melting followed by appropriate heat treatment is a suitable processing route for producing the proposed SCCP microstructure.
The proposed structural mediator is the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates and their coherent interfaces with the matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve local stress concentrations.
Relieving stress concentrations delays premature crack initiation.
Improved dislocation transmission and delayed cracking permit enhanced plastic deformation and tensile ductility.
The modified alloy will attain ambient-temperature tensile ductility above approximately 10–15%.
The modified alloy will maintain ultrahigh strength while attaining improved ductility.
The ductility improvement depends on processing and composition remaining within a window that produces the coherent nanoprecipitate structure.
The precise composition and processing thresholds for optimizing nanoprecipitation and ductility have not been determined.
SEM and EBSD can confirm the presence and distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes nanoprecipitation during processing at ambient conditions, whereas the proposed arc-melting and heat-treatment route necessarily involves elevated-temperature processing.
